candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 42:1 (Joseph reveals himself (42:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee a famine began to come into the land, and the rain refused to be given to the earth, for none whatever fell' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 42:1 famine context. The Tewahedo agrarian-monastic tradition reads famine-narratives canonically: corporate suffering is the divine instrument for canonical-reunification (Jacob's family is reunified through famine-driven travel). The Tewahedo täzkar-ǝgziʾabəḥer (commemoration of God) tradition during years of agricultural distress draws on the Joseph-famine pattern: collective suffering as the matrix of providential mercy preparing reconciliation.

candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 42:16 (Joseph reveals himself (42:16)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And he commanded that he should keep one of them in prison, but the others he sent away with corn, and he said: bring Benjamin to me' — Joseph's demand for Benjamin's presence as the condition for the brothers' return preserves the Gen 42 narrative. Tewahedo canonical-reading: the demand-for-Benjamin is functionally the demand-for-Jacob's-fully-trusting-the-arrangement, since Benjamin is Jacob's last-remaining-child-of-Rachel and is dearer than even Joseph was. The Tewahedo pastoral pattern of asking the penitent to entrust the most precious thing as the canonical-test of repentance draws on this canonical OT pattern.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee a famine began to come into the land, and the rain refused to be given to the earth, for none whatever fell' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 42:1 famine context. The Tewahedo agrarian-monastic tradition reads famine-narratives canonically: corporate suffering is the divine instrument for canonical-reunification (Jacob's family is reunified through famine-driven travel). The Tewahedo täzkar-ǝgziʾabəḥer (commemoration of God) tradition during years of agricultural distress draws on the Joseph-famine pattern: collective suffering as the matrix of providential mercy preparing reconciliation.
